expectations.text: executive_narrative.md exists and its main body is at most about 600 words (readable in roughly 3 minutes).
expectations.evidence: File exists in B/work/. wc -w = 635 whole file; 627 excluding the H1; about 613 excluding headings and about 576 excluding headings, footer and meta line. Within 'about 600', the same standard as A.

expectations.text: The first paragraph states the central conclusion (e.g. growth is price-driven / full-year forecast at risk) rather than background or an introduction.
expectations.evidence: First paragraph (bold): 'Our +4% growth is less healthy than it looks. Prices are carrying it, and so is inventory we've pushed into customers. Consumers are buying fewer of our products, and the full-year forecast of $548M doesn't yet include the inventory correction that customers have told us is coming.'

expectations.text: It states that the +4.0% year-over-year growth is price-driven (price +6.8%) while volume declined (-3.1%).
expectations.evidence: 'Price is the only thing growing. Price contributed +6.8% and volume fell -3.1%. The budget assumed +4.5% price and +1.5% volume.' The +4.0% sits in the next paragraph.

expectations.text: It identifies the sell-in (+4.0%) vs sell-out (+0.7%) gap and trade inventory of 6.8 weeks against the agreed 4-6 week range as a risk to Q4 / the full-year forecast.
expectations.evidence: Item 2: 'Sell-in grew +4.0%, but consumer sell-out grew only +0.7%'; inventory 'from 5.2 to 6.8 weeks of supply, above the agreed 4-6 week range'; customers will cut back by year-end; 'it is not in the forecast'. The $548M, the $8M gap to budget and 'probably the best case' are stated in the bottom line.

expectations.text: Any figure not stated in the source (e.g. ~$12.6M exposure = 1.6 extra weeks x $7.9M/week, or a revised full-year number) is labeled as an estimate or calculation and its basis is shown; no number contradicts the source.
expectations.evidence: The destock figures are labeled with their basis: 'getting back to 6 weeks removes about $6M ... 5-week midpoint ... about $14M', plus the footer 'The destock estimates ($6-14M) are derived: excess weeks of supply x $7.9M weekly sell-out' and the retail-value caveat. I checked them: 0.8 x 7.9 = 6.3 and 1.8 x 7.9 = 14.2. It gives no revised full-year number or $12.6M build figure, which the assertion lists only as examples. Minor gap: 'about $12M lost vs prior year' for Digestia is derived and untagged. 'Digestia is the main reason the Midwest is 4.2% below budget' is unsupported, since the source cites weather, competition and the delisting. 'Now that repeat purchase has proven the product' overstates a repeat rate that is only 'in line with' the benchmark. No number contradicts the source.

expectations.text: It flags the deterioration in trade promotion effectiveness (average ROI 0.82 vs 1.07, 3 of 11 national promotions below 1.0, and/or trade spend +18%).
expectations.evidence: Item 3: 'Trade spend is up 18% to $58.4M. Average promotion ROI fell from 1.07 to 0.82 ... Brevex BOGO returned 0.61 and Relivia 30% off returned 0.74.' It does not mention 3 of 11 below 1.0, but the assertion needs only one of the listed signals.

expectations.text: It ends with specific actions or decisions (e.g. reset Q4 sell-in / forecast, stop or redesign negative-ROI promotions, Somnis recovery, OTIF fix), not generic statements like 'continue to monitor'.
expectations.evidence: Closes with 'Decisions for Monday', five specific decisions framed as questions: reforecast with the destock and stop shipping above range in Q4; pause or redesign ROI<1.0 promotions before the Q4/Q1 calendar locks; Digestia (close the private-label gap, re-pack value range, manage for cash, recover MegaMart Midwest); Somnis (push ACV from 41% toward 70%); Columbus supply fix and the $1.9M fines. No placeholders.

expectations.text: It contains no generic filler (e.g. 'in today's rapidly evolving landscape', 'holistic overview') and does not repeat the source's unsupported 'solid performance' framing as fact.
expectations.evidence: No filler phrases. It rejects the report's 'solid performance' framing with 'less healthy than it looks' and does not repeat it as fact.

strengths: Clean, readable structure: a bold bottom line, six numbered findings, a short 'what's working', and five decisions for Monday. No placeholders, so it is ready to use, and the destock estimate is labeled derived with its basis in the footer.

Explicitly rejects the report's 'solid performance' conclusion and leads with the price-versus-volume and sell-in versus sell-out story. Includes the 0.82 vs 1.07 ROI, the +18% trade spend and the two largest promotions' ROIs.
Decisions are specific and broader (Digestia options, Columbus and the fines, Somnis ACV), framed as questions suited to a leadership meeting.
The chat reply is concise, clearly says the $6-14M figure and the decisions are the assistant's own, and flags the 14.1% 'gross sales' inconsistency.
defects: Gives no revised full-year figure and no quantified forecast exposure beyond the $6-14M destock range, so the headline risk is less actionable than A's. The 'Q4 orders' framing mixes retail value with shipments, though it caveats this.

Unsupported or overstated claims: 'Digestia is the main reason the Midwest is 4.2% below budget' (the source cites weather and competition as well); 'repeat purchase has proven the product' (34% is only in line with the benchmark); 'about $12M lost' for Digestia is derived and untagged.
Repeats the source's 0.82 average ROI without noticing that it is inconsistent with only 3 of 11 promotions below 1.0, and omits the '3 of 11' fact.
Slightly longer on lower-priority items (six findings plus 'what's working'), with less prioritization of which decisions matter most.
